name: Government Blacksmith Shop

documented_range.note: NO SOURCE DATES THIS BUILDING AT EITHER END; both dates are the honest bounds of what is attested. THE START: Andreas says only 'After the second Fort Dearborn was built, David McKee was appointed Government blacksmith, his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street' — the fort was rebuilt in 1816 — but the same book fixes McKee's arrival: he was engaged as the agency blacksmith the 1821 treaty required and, by his own recollection, reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, finding 'but two houses on the north side of the river' and building the fourth himself. 1823 is therefore the first year the shop can have stood under him, and the range opens there rather than at 1816. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM. The shop is attested standing around 1830 — 'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' — and in 1831 Wau-Bun still describes the ring of agency log residences with a blacksmith among them. After that nothing. McKee himself had other work by then; he was carrying the Government mail to Fort Wayne monthly from 1827-28 and later farmed on the Des Plaines. A GOVERNMENT SMITH WAS STILL OWED TO THE POTAWATOMI IN 1835 under the 1821 and 1833 treaties, which is the argument for the shop still standing on the scene date, and it is an argument about an obligation rather than about a building. Tagged inferred for that reason.

position.symbolic_location: North side, near the Agency House at the foot of State Street, on the riverbank strip west of the agency house.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-11 AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING, NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. What is attested is proximity and a foot of a street: Andreas, 'his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street'; the 1825 tax list gloss, 'David McKee lived on the North Side, near the agency-house of Dr. Wolcott'; the Scott family notice, 'lived on the north side of the river near the foot of what is now North State Street'; and Wau-Bun's ring — 'Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers.' Method: this record's coordinate is set 32 m west of this project's cobweb_castle placement, on the same riverbank strip, its south face 16 m north of the drawn 1834 bank. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE INVENTED. 'Near' is unquantified and no source says which side of the agency house the smithy stood on; west was chosen because it keeps the shop inside the ring the sources describe and off the State Street frontage, and it could as easily have been north or east. Working uncertainty about 40 m — the georeference's 20 m plus the unquantified 'near'. A COMPETING PLACEMENT IS ON THE RECORD AND IS NOT ADOPTED: one of Andreas's recollections of the 1820s puts 'the blacksmith shop of David McKee and Joseph Porthick (Porthier)' next to a double log house 'nearly opposite the fort' occupied jointly by John Kinzie and Alexander Wolcott, which is the Kinzie house cluster some 400 m further east. Three statements name the agency house or the foot of State Street against that one, so the outlier is treated as a conflation of the two north-bank clusters. Facade bearing 180, due south, follows the agency house it is grouped with; nothing states it. There is no modelled terrain under this building — it stands about 450 m east of the terrain box.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 6 x 4.5 m is about 20 x 15 ft, a one-fire smithy: room for a forge, an anvil and a horse. Every number is invented. Andreas's one editorial remark about the scale of the place — 'David McKee's little shop and scant kit of tools bore but a slight family resemblance to the machine shops and rolling mills of to-day' — is the whole of the evidence for 'small', and it is a comparison, not a measurement.

construction.note: Wau-Bun describes the buildings round the agency house as 'a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers'; Andreas records the 1830 north bank as having 'small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' in the agency house's vicinity, and McKee's own account of the houses he found and built there — 'All these houses were of logs'. Note that the first two describe the blacksmith's RESIDENCE among the group; that the shop was of the same fabric is the reading, and it is the only fabric anybody reports on this ground in these years.

stories.note: Not attested, and about as safe as an inference gets: a smithy is a single tall room with a forge in it, and every building in this group is described as small and log.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.4 m is about 8 ft, a single-pen log wall — the same reading this project gives the Sauganash's 1829 cabin. A working smithy might well have been built taller to carry the heat and the smoke, which is an argument nobody's source makes and which would raise this number if it were ever attested.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested, and the reasoning here is a trade's rather than a household's: a forge has to vent, so a smithy carries a stack whatever else it lacks. WHAT THE MODEL SHOWS IS A DOMESTIC CHIMNEY. The archetype builds one 0.96 m square shaft with a corbelled head against the gable end — the same stack it builds on a dwelling — so nothing in the mesh distinguishes a forge flue from a cabin's fireplace, and nothing in the mesh says a smithy. That is admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md rather than hidden.

phases.change_note: The Government blacksmith's shop of the Chicago agency, standing near the agency house at the foot of State Street from about 1823, when David McKee arrived to fill the post the 1821 treaty required. McKee's later work as mail-carrier and his removal to the Des Plaines are changes of occupation and do not open new phases.

function.note: 'David McKee was appointed Government blacksmith, his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street' — Andreas, opening his chapter on the town's early manufactories with it, since a blacksmith is where the manufacturing history of the place starts. WHO WAS WORKING IT ON THE SCENE DATE IS UNATTESTED: McKee had been carrying the mail since 1827-28, the 1830-31 agency staffing lists him as blacksmith with Joseph Porthier as striker, and nothing reached names a smith here in 1835. The record therefore carries no occupants block.

research_note: A BUILDING KNOWN ONLY AS A CLAUSE IN OTHER PEOPLE'S SENTENCES, and one of the few in this dataset whose existence rests on four independent statements while nothing at all is known of its shape. It belongs to the agency establishment: the 1821 treaty obliged the Government to keep a blacksmith at Chicago for the Potawatomi, McKee was hired for that and arrived in 1823, and Wau-Bun's ring of log residences round Cobweb Castle is the same cluster seen from 1831. THE RECORD IS FLAGGED review_required for the reason AGENTS.md gives: the smithy exists because of a treaty obligation to the Potawatomi, and that is Indigenous history whatever the building looked like. Nothing here depicts or narrates it. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THE RECORD: agency accounts or the Indian Office's returns, which paid for the shop and its iron and would describe both; failing that, any of the recollections that place the north-bank cluster building by building. See docs/RESEARCH/blacksmith_shop_state_st.md.
